findings.claim: One user says release notes stop being a dev artifact and become a communication channel

quotes.text: If you're talking to users, Release notes stop being a dev artifact and become a communication channel.

review: the quoted text does not share two key words with the brief, including one about the problem or idea rather than the customer, so it is not counted as evidence about it
notes: not sent to the model: off-topic for this brief

findings.claim: One user says an AI agent could spend a lot of time writing v1 code, having it fail and iterate to v2 and then to v3

quotes.text: If anyone wants to use an AI agent to try out PyInfra - One issue I've faced is that PyInfra was rearchitected in v2 (and some more in v3?) but what belongs in v1 vs v2 vs v3 isn't very clear, so an AI agent could spend a lot of time writing v1 code, having it fail and iterate to v2 and then to v3.

findings.reason: The quote directly states that an AI agent could spend time writing v1 code, failing, and iterating to v2 and v3 due to unclear version boundaries.
findings.limitations: Single user experience, not generalizable to all AI agents or codebases.

findings.claim: Small software teams spend too much time writing release notes and changelogs.

quotes.text: Now she translates software engineering bug fix reports into customer-appropriate release notes for a big process-automation company.

findings.reason: The quote shows one person's experience with writing release notes, but the claim is about small software teams generally.
findings.limitations: One person's experience, not generalizing to small teams.
review: wording goes beyond the quoted text: small, teams, spend, too, much, time, writing, changelogs
a claim about people must be attributed to one person ("One host says ...")
